Working with priors

2026-10-15

Source: vignettes/priors.Rmd
priors.Rmd

NOTE: the JAGS-specific prior interface below is likely to be deprecated in the future, when additional backends are added beyond JAGS.

This article is about setting your own priors.

To learn more about priors when you do not set them yourself, read more about the mcp default priors. Briefly, mcp assigns default priors to all parameters that you do not set. These are the conventional defaults of rstanarm for intercepts and coefficients and of brms for scale parameters, with mcp-specific defaults for change points and autocorrelation. Inspect them using prior_summary(fit).

Setting a prior

mcp takes priors in the form of a named list. The names are the parameter names, and the values are distribution strings, fixed values, or the names of other parameters. Here is a fairly complicated example, to demonstrate the various ways priors can be used:

model = list(
  y ~ 1 + x,  # Intercept_1 + x_1
  ~ 1 + x,  # cp_1, Intercept_2, and x_2
  ~ 1 + x  # cp_2
)

prior = list(
  Intercept_1 = "dnorm(0, 5) T(, 10)",  # Intercept; less than 10
  x_1 = "dbeta(2, 5)",  # slope: beta with right skew
  cp_1 = "dnorm(30, 10)",  # change point around 30 (and before cp_2)
  x_2 = "dt(0, 1, 3) T(x_1, )",  # slope 2 > slope 1 and t-distributed
  cp_2 = 80,  # A constant (set; not estimated)
  x_3 = "x_2"  # same slope as x_2 (use same() instead; see below)
  # Intercept_2 and Intercept_3 not specified. Use default.
)

Distribution strings use JAGS names and argument order, including T() truncation, so JAGS distributions are generally allowed (see the JAGS user manual). However, they are not JAGS code: mcp uses conventional scales instead of JAGS precision, i.e., SD for dnorm(), SD on the log scale for dlnorm() (sdlog in stats::dlnorm()), and scale for dt(), ddexp(), and dlogis(). When generating JAGS code, mcp converts these to inverse variance for dnorm(), dt(), and dlnorm(), and inverse scale for ddexp() and dlogis(). You can inspect the translation by comparing fit$prior with fit$jags_code.

Other notes:

  • Change points are always ordered (cp_1 < cp_2 < ...), whatever their priors. See priors on change points.

  • mcp allows inserting data-dependent terms: for example, min(x), max(x), mean(y), median(y), sd(y), mad(y), max(x) - min(x), n_segments(), and n_cp(). mcp resolves these expressions before generating JAGS code. The older mcp v0.3.4 uppercase constants (MINX, MAXX, and so on) remain temporarily supported with a deprecation warning.

  • You can fix any parameter to a specific value. Simply set it to a numerical value (as cp_2 above). A constant is a 100% prior belief in that value, and it will therefore not be estimated.

  • To reuse a coefficient in a later segment, prefer same() in the model, e.g., ~ 1 + same(x) in segment 3. This reuses x_2 instead of estimating x_3. Equating parameters in the prior (x_3 = "x_2" above) gives the same fit but keeps x_3 as a duplicate. Read more about same() in Understanding mcp formulas.

  • You can write deterministic expressions such as x_3 = "x_2 + 5 - cp_1/10". Since x_3 is now deterministic given x_2 and cp_1, this leaves one fewer free parameter to estimate.

Let us see the priors after running them through mcp and compare to the default priors:

library(mcp)
df_dummy = data.frame(x = 1:100, y = 1:100)
empty_manual = mcp(model, data = df_dummy, prior = prior, sample = FALSE)
empty_default = mcp(model, data = df_dummy, sample = FALSE)

# Inspect resolved priors and their bounds
prior_summary(empty_manual)  # For more details: add verbose = TRUE
## # A tibble: 9 × 5
##   parameter   segment dpar  prior                                         bounds           
##   <chr>         <int> <chr> <chr>                                         <chr>            
## 1 cp_1              2 NA    normal(mean = 30, sd = 10)                    [1, 100], ordered
## 2 cp_2              3 NA    80                                            none             
## 3 Intercept_1       1 mu    normal(mean = 0, sd = 5)                      [-Inf, 10]       
## 4 x_1               1 mu    beta(shape1 = 2, shape2 = 5)                  [0, 1]           
## 5 Intercept_2       2 mu    normal(mean = 50.5, sd = 72.529)              none             
## 6 x_2               2 mu    student_t(df = 3, location = 0, scale = 1)    [x_1, Inf]       
## 7 Intercept_3       3 mu    normal(mean = 50.5, sd = 72.529)              none             
## 8 x_3               3 mu    x_2                                           none             
## 9 sigma_1           1 sigma student_t(df = 3, location = 0, scale = 37.1) [0, Inf]
prior_summary(empty_default)  # For more details: add verbose = TRUE
## # A tibble: 9 × 5
##   parameter   segment dpar  prior                                         bounds           
##   <chr>         <int> <chr> <chr>                                         <chr>            
## 1 cp_1              2 NA    uniform(min = 1, max = 100)                   [1, 100], ordered
## 2 cp_2              3 NA    uniform(min = 1, max = 100)                   [1, 100], ordered
## 3 Intercept_1       1 mu    normal(mean = 50.5 - x_1 * 1, sd = 72.529)    none             
## 4 x_1               1 mu    normal(mean = 0, sd = 2.5)                    none             
## 5 Intercept_2       2 mu    normal(mean = 50.5, sd = 72.529)              none             
## 6 x_2               2 mu    normal(mean = 0, sd = 2.5)                    none             
## 7 Intercept_3       3 mu    normal(mean = 50.5, sd = 72.529)              none             
## 8 x_3               3 mu    normal(mean = 0, sd = 2.5)                    none             
## 9 sigma_1           1 sigma student_t(df = 3, location = 0, scale = 37.1) [0, Inf]

Now, let’s simulate some data from model. The following priors are “at odds” with the actual data so as to show their effect.

df = data.frame(x = runif(200, 0, 100), y = 1)  # 200 datapoints between 0 and 100
df$y = empty_default$simulate(empty_default, df, 
    Intercept_1 = 20, Intercept_2 = 22, Intercept_3 = 30,  # intercepts
    x_1 = -0.5, x_2 = 0.5, x_3 = 0,  # slopes
    cp_1 = 35, cp_2 = 70,  # change points
    sigma = 5)

head(df)
##          x        y
## 1 91.48060 36.00483
## 2 93.70754 35.22376
## 3 28.61395  0.67698
## 4 83.04476 39.24241
## 5 64.17455 33.25341
## 6 51.90959 30.98237

Sample the prior and posterior.

future::plan(future::multisession, workers = 3)
fit_manual = mcp(model, data = df, sample = "both", prior = prior)
fit_default = mcp(model, data = df, sample = "both")

First, let’s look at the priors side by side. Notice the use of prior = TRUE to show prior draws. This works in plot(), plot_pars(), and summary() among others.

library(ggplot2)
pp_default = plot_pars(fit_default, type = "dens_overlay", prior = TRUE, npars = NULL) + 
  ggtitle("Default priors")

pp_manual = plot_pars(fit_manual, type = "dens_overlay", prior = TRUE, npars = NULL) +
  ggtitle("Manual priors")

pp_default + pp_manual

Here are the resulting posterior fits:

plot_default = plot(fit_default) + ggtitle("Default priors")

plot_manual = plot(fit_manual) + ggtitle("Manual priors")

plot_default + plot_manual

We see the effects of the priors:

  • The intercept Intercept_1 was truncated to be below 10.
  • The slope x_1 is restricted to the bounds of dbeta(), i.e., between 0 and 1.
  • The slopes x_2 and x_3 were forced to be identical.
  • The change point cp_2 was a constant, so there is no uncertainty there. cp_1 is still ordered before it, i.e., its prior is dnorm(30, 10) restricted to min(x) < cp_1 < 80.

Adding verbose = TRUE reveals full details including the rule descriptions, parameter classifications (kind), and whether each prior came from the user or data-calibrated defaults:

prior_summary(fit_manual, verbose = TRUE)
## # A tibble: 9 × 9
##   parameter   segment dpar  prior                                        bounds                     rule                                                                description                                                                                     source  kind        
##   <chr>         <int> <chr> <chr>                                        <chr>                      <chr>                                                               <chr>                                                                                           <chr>   <chr>       
## 1 cp_1              2 NA    normal(mean = 30, sd = 10)                   [0.02389, 98.889], ordered normal(mean = 30, sd = 10)                                          User-specified prior, truncated to the observed range of x, restricted to ordered change points user    distribution
## 2 cp_2              3 NA    80                                           none                       80                                                                  Fixed at 80                                                                                     user    constant    
## 3 Intercept_1       1 mu    normal(mean = 0, sd = 5)                     [-Inf, 10]                 normal(mean = 0, sd = 5)                                            User-specified prior                                                                            user    distribution
## 4 x_1               1 mu    beta(shape1 = 2, shape2 = 5)                 [0, 1]                     beta(shape1 = 2, shape2 = 5)                                        User-specified prior                                                                            user    distribution
## 5 Intercept_2       2 mu    normal(mean = 24.322, sd = 26.856)           none                       normal(mean = mean(y), sd = 2.5 * sd(y))                            Mean intercept (rstanarm default)                                                               default distribution
## 6 x_2               2 mu    student_t(df = 3, location = 0, scale = 1)   [x_1, Inf]                 student_t(df = 3, location = 0, scale = 1)                          User-specified prior                                                                            user    distribution
## 7 Intercept_3       3 mu    normal(mean = 24.322, sd = 26.856)           none                       normal(mean = mean(y), sd = 2.5 * sd(y))                            Mean intercept (rstanarm default)                                                               default distribution
## 8 x_3               3 mu    x_2                                          none                       x_2                                                                 Same value as x_2                                                                               user    alias       
## 9 sigma_1           1 sigma student_t(df = 3, location = 0, scale = 9.9) [0, Inf]                   student_t(df = 3, location = 0, scale = max(2.5, round(mad(y), 1))) Positive residual SD calibrated on the response scale                                           default distribution

This is a contrived example. Usually setting priors manually aims to sample the “correct” posterior.

Prior predictive checks

Prior predictive checks are a great way to ensure that the priors are meaningful before fitting to data. Simply set sample = "prior". Let us do it for the manual and default priors above to compare their prior predictive space:

# Sample priors
fit_pp_manual = mcp(model, data = df, prior = prior, sample = "prior")
fit_pp_default = mcp(model, data = df, sample = "prior")

# Plot it
plot_pp_manual = plot(fit_pp_manual, lines = 100, prior = TRUE) + ylim(c(-400, 400)) + ggtitle("Manual prior")
plot_pp_default = plot(fit_pp_default, lines = 100, prior = TRUE) + ylim(c(-400, 400)) + ggtitle("Default prior")
plot_pp_manual + plot_pp_default  # using patchwork

You can see how the manual priors force strictly positive slopes (x_2 > x_1 > 0) that compound to span a much wider vertical range than the defaults, alongside an abrupt concerted change at the fixed change point x = 80. In contrast, the default priors are centered on the observed data, with zero-centered slopes and change points distributed smoothly across the x range.

Priors on change points

Change points are always ordered, cp_1 < cp_2 < ... < cp_n. Without this, the segments could swap places between draws (“label switching”), and the change points would not be identifiable. In mcp, each change point keeps its specified prior, restricted to ordered change points. cp_1 always has the prior specified for cp_1. When change points have group-level deviations, their locations are additionally ordered within every group.

The default prior on change points is a flat Dirichlet prior on the segment lengths, also known as “uniform order statistics”. The article on default priors describes it and its math.

Inspecting priors on change points

  • fit$prior and prior_summary(fit) show the prior specified for each change point. The default is dunif(min(x), max(x)) on each change point, i.e., a uniform distribution on the observed range of par_x. In fit$prior, min(x) and max(x) are written as cp_0 and cp_K, e.g., cp_3 with two change points. prior_summary(fit) shows them as numbers, and its bounds column marks change points as “ordered”. prior_summary(fit, verbose = TRUE) describes which restrictions mcp applied.
  • plot_pars(fit, prior = TRUE) shows the marginal priors, i.e., after the ordering. Where the specified priors overlap, the marginal priors differ from them. For example, the default priors on cp_1 and cp_2 in the plot above are not flat but triangular, because cp_1 must be before cp_2. Use mcp(..., sample = "prior") or sample = "both" to get prior draws.
  • fit$jags_code shows how JAGS samples them. See From formulas to sampler code.

Setting priors on change points

You can set priors on change points as shown in the initial example. Here are the rules:

  • Lower and upper bounds. Priors without dunif() or T() are truncated to the observed range of x, e.g., dnorm(30, 10) becomes dnorm(30, 10) T(min(x), max(x)). The lower and upper bounds that you set in dunif() or T() are used unchanged, also beyond the data, e.g., to place a change point in the future as in this forecasting example. JAGS cannot truncate dunif(), so set its bounds as its arguments instead of using T().
  • Minimum segment lengths. To make the segment between cp_1 and cp_2 at least 20 long, write the previous change point plus the length as the lower bound: cp_2 = "dunif(cp_1 + 20, max(x))" or cp_2 = "dnorm(70, 10) T(cp_1 + 20, )". An empty upper bound defaults to max(x). Like the ordering, the minimum segment length is a restriction, not JAGS’s renormalizing truncation T(cp_1 + 20, ). Other references to change points in the lower and upper bounds are errors, because change points are already ordered. A lower bound of just the previous change point, e.g., dunif(cp_1, max(x)) as in mcp v0.3, is not needed and gives a warning.
  • Fixed change points such as cp_2 = 80 are also ordered, i.e., cp_1 stays below 80.
  • Conditional priors. Priors can refer to other change points in their distribution parameters, e.g., cp_3 = "dnorm(cp_2 + 30, 10)". Each change point then has its prior given the change points it refers to, still restricted to ordered change points. If JAGS stops with “Slicer stuck at value with infinite density”, the conditional prior has (practically) no probability within its lower and upper bounds for some values of the change points it refers to. Widen the prior or its bounds.
  • Regular spacing. cp_1 = "dirichlet(2)" sets a Dirichlet prior with \alpha = 2 on all change points, which makes short segments less likely and so favors evenly spaced change points away from the ends of the observed range. \alpha = 1 is the default prior. All change points share the same \alpha, so it cannot be combined with other priors on change points. See the math.
  • Initial values. All chains start at the same, equally spaced change points, moved inside the bounds of their priors if needed. Set other initial values using, e.g., mcp(..., inits = list(cp_1 = 30)), as long as they are ordered. More details on initialization in the implementation article.

JAGS code

Here is the JAGS code for fit_manual:

fit_manual$jags_code
## model {
##   # Change points
##   cp_0 = min(x)
##   cp_1 ~ dnorm(30, 1/(10)^2) T(cp_0,cp_3)  # User-specified prior, truncated to the observed range of x, restricted to ordered change points
##   cp_2 = 80  # Fixed at 80
##   cp_3 = max(x)
##   cp_order_ ~ dbern(step(cp_2 - cp_1))  # Ordered change points
## 
##   # Priors for population-level effects
##   Intercept_1 ~ dnorm(0, 1/(5)^2) T(,10)  # User-specified prior
##   x_1 ~ dbeta(2, 5)  # User-specified prior
##   Intercept_2_end_ ~ dnorm(24.321850954171083 + x_2 * (cp_2 - cp_1), 1/(26.856367009148308)^2)   # Mean intercept (rstanarm default); sampled as the value at the segment end
##   Intercept_2 = Intercept_2_end_ - (x_2 * (cp_2 - cp_1))
##   x_2 ~ dt(0, 1/(1)^2, 3) T(x_1,)  # User-specified prior
##   Intercept_3_end_ ~ dnorm(24.321850954171083 + x_3 * (cp_3 - cp_2), 1/(26.856367009148308)^2)   # Mean intercept (rstanarm default); sampled as the value at the segment end
##   Intercept_3 = Intercept_3_end_ - (x_3 * (cp_3 - cp_2))
##   x_3 = x_2  # Same value as x_2
##   sigma_1 ~ dt(0, 1/(9.9)^2, 3) T(0,)  # Positive residual SD calibrated on the response scale
## 
##   # Model and likelihood
##   for (i_ in 1:length(x)) {
##     # par_x local to each segment
##     x_local_1_[i_] = min(x[i_], cp_1)
##     x_local_2_[i_] = min(x[i_], cp_2) - cp_1
##     x_local_3_[i_] = min(x[i_], cp_3) - cp_2
##     
##     # Formula for mu
##     link_mu_[i_] =
##       (x[i_] >= cp_0) * (x[i_] < cp_1) * inprod(rhs_matrix_[i_, c(1)], c(Intercept_1)) * 1 + 
##       (x[i_] >= cp_0) * (x[i_] < cp_1) * inprod(rhs_matrix_[i_, c(2)], c(x_1)) * x_local_1_[i_] + 
##       (x[i_] >= cp_1) * (x[i_] < cp_2) * inprod(rhs_matrix_[i_, c(3)], c(Intercept_2)) * 1 + 
##       (x[i_] >= cp_1) * (x[i_] < cp_2) * inprod(rhs_matrix_[i_, c(4)], c(x_2)) * x_local_2_[i_] + 
##       (x[i_] >= cp_2) * inprod(rhs_matrix_[i_, c(5)], c(Intercept_3)) * 1 + 
##       (x[i_] >= cp_2) * inprod(rhs_matrix_[i_, c(6)], c(x_3)) * x_local_3_[i_]
##     
##     # Formula for sigma
##     link_sigma_[i_] =
##       (x[i_] >= cp_0) * inprod(rhs_matrix_[i_, c(7)], c(sigma_1)) * 1
## 
##     # Likelihood for family = gaussian()
##     mu_[i_] = link_mu_[i_]
##     sigma_[i_] = max(1e-05, link_sigma_[i_])
##     y[i_] ~ dnorm(mu_[i_], 1 / sigma_[i_]^2)
##   }
## }
